extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners concerned with scientific method, logic, and induction (philosophy of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for forming, describing, and using observations and general conceptions in induction; how to abstract, classify, and test hypotheses through comparison of phenomena. Emphasizes discrimination between sensation and inference, the formation of appropriate conceptions, and the tentative nature of abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation from inference
rubrics_metrics.description: That what is supposed to have been observed shall really have been observed; that it be an observation, not an inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Saying 'I hear a man's voice' conflates perception and inference — the direct perception is only 'I hear a sound,' while that it is a voice and a man's voice are inferences. Saying 'I saw my brother' really rests on visual sensations plus inference from resemblance and past experience. The guidance is to scrutinize reports of observation to separate raw sensory content from the inferential attributions about causes or identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation extends only to sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation extends only to the sensations by which we recognize objects; propositions which we make use of, either in science or in common life, relate mostly to the objects themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that every act of observation includes at least one inference (from sensation to object, or from marks/diagnostics to whole phenomenon). In practice, record the sensations and explicitly note any inferential steps used to attribute them to objects or causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors of sense are erroneous inferences (not sense failures)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no errors of sense properly so called; they are erroneous inferences from sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: optical deceptions (kaleidoscope), tactile illusions (crossed fingers feeling two marbles), hallucinations, dreams. In each case the sensations themselves are genuine; the error lies in the judgment that ascribes those sensations to an incorrect external cause. Thus, when evaluating reports or data, focus on whether the inference from sensation to cause is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic of observation: discriminate sensations versus inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic of observation consists solely in a correct discrimination between that, in a result of observation, which has really been perceived, and that which is an inference from the perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, strip observational reports down to feelings or states of consciousness (outward sensations and inward feelings), and treat any statements about external objects or their properties as inferential claims to be separately evaluated by inductive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions necessarily assert more than perceptions (classification implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the simplest description of an observation, there is, and must always be, much more asserted than is contained in the perception itself: to describe is to affirm a connection between the observed sensation and other things denoted or connoted by the terms used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Saying 'I see something white' not only reports a sensation but also classes it with other 'white' things—asserting resemblance. When documenting observations, be explicit about the classificatory concepts you apply and aware that description imports prior conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and description introduce conceptions not found in raw perception
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inherent in a description to be the statement of a resemblance, or resemblances; something is introduced which was not included in the observation itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moving from sensation to linguistic description, make explicit the general conception used to assimilate the sensation to a class (e.g., 'white thing'), because those conceptions supply the materials for induction and may themselves require justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and many 'observations' include deductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When I assert a measurement (e.g., the animal measures ten feet) the fact is not an immediate perception but a conclusion from reasoning; the minor premises alone being furnished by observation of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat measurements as combined observational + deductive claims. Record the instruments, auxiliary assumptions (units, arithmetic), and inferential steps used in producing measurements so they can be scrutinized in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation of facts (hypotheses) is preliminary to induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Colligation of facts by means of hypotheses (conceptions) is not induction itself but a subsidiary operation: it ascertains in what circumstances the observed instances agree and supplies the prerequisites for induction by methods like Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize hypothesis-formation (finding a pattern or resemblance among observations) as a distinct step from inductive generalization; evaluate hypotheses by how well they reveal common circumstances among observed instances and enable induction on unobserved cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: General conceptions are necessary instruments for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Such notions or conceptions do exist; the mind can conceive a multitude of individual things as one assemblage or class, and general names suggest to us certain ideas or mental representations which represent the whole class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that when forming inductive arguments you identify the general conception in play (the class or predicate) and how it represents or stands for the class of phenomena under study. These conceptions are the medium of general reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions are often formed by abstraction from the phenomena themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception originally found its way to us as the result of comparison; it was obtained by abstraction from individual things, sometimes from the very facts which it later colligates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that key analytical concepts may be derived from the data through careful comparison. Document the comparative process that produced a conception (which items were compared, which features noted) to justify its adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sometimes conceptions must be superinduced (preexisting ideas required)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some difficult cases (e.g., Kepler's ellipse) the conception had to be brought to the facts — it could not be evolved from them; the idea was superinduced upon the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cases where prior theoretical/conceptual frameworks are necessary from cases where concepts can be abstracted from observations. When prior conceptions are used, justify their origin and assess their plausibility to avoid circularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must be clear and appropriate to the matter in hand
rubrics_metrics.description: To perform induction well, our general conceptions must be 'clear' and 'appropriate' to the matter in hand; inappropriate conceptions miss important agreements or fix on trifling or imaginary agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate conceptions for clarity (unambiguous content) and appropriateness (relevance to the phenomena and to the explanatory questions at hand). Example: classifying animals by skeleton structure is more appropriate for structural/habit studies than classifying by color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison requires a type or standard as a practical condition of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: When objects are more than two, a type of some sort is an indispensable condition of the comparison; we fix upon one object as our standard and compare others to it, leading to stages of abstraction and conception formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In empirical work, specify the standard or exemplar used for comparison (why chosen, which features considered). Be ready to shift the type/standard if it yields inconclusive or irrelevant agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction and conception formation is a tentative, iterative process
rubrics_metrics.description: We find the right conception by a tentative process, trying first one and then another until we hit the mark; if unsatisfied with agreements discovered, we change our path and form different general conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt iterative methods in concept formation: propose a conception, test its reach across instances, and revise or abandon it if it fails to capture the important agreements. Document alternative conceptions tried and reasons for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware inappropriate abstractions that produce false generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: An inappropriate conception may include cases not belonging to the phenomenon and exclude genuine cases (e.g., Aristotle's 'moving toward its own place' misclassifies spontaneous motion); such inappropriate abstraction leads to error or plurality of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether a chosen conception captures all and only the cases relevant to the phenomenon; check for counterexamples and hidden heterogeneity that indicate the need for multiple causes or different classificatory schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive generalizations can be more reliable than single observations
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition collected from particulars is often more certainly true than any one of the particular propositions from which it was inferred, because each particular involved inference errors which chance is unlikely to reproduce across many instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing inductions, weigh the number and independence of instances: multiple independent instances reduce the likelihood that a common inference error produced the pattern. Still, scrutinize underlying inferences in each instance to rule out systematic bias.
